missions/majority-world-missions/name: Majority-world sending movements (Nigeria, Brazil, India, Philippines; ‘from everywhere to everywhere’)
missions/majority-world-missions/statusN: Active and expanding: by around 2010 Brazil, South Korea and India were among the ten largest sending countries, and much of the world’s missionary force now comes from Africa, Asia and Latin America — though many majority-world workers serve within their own countries or diasporas, and statistics remain uncertain.
missions/majority-world-missions/summary: In the twentieth century the churches planted by Western missions — and many that arose independently — began to send missionaries of their own, first to neighbouring peoples and then across the world. Indian, Nigerian, Ghanaian, Brazilian, Korean, Filipino and Chinese Christians built agencies, denominational mission boards and migrant church networks, so that by the early twenty-first century mission was, in Michael Nazir-Ali’s phrase, ‘from everywhere to everywhere’. The movement brought cultural closeness, lower costs and fresh energy, and challenged the assumption that mission meant the West going to the rest; it also reproduced some old problems and exported new ones, notably prosperity teaching.
missions/majority-world-missions/story:
Non-Western Christians had always carried the faith — Pacific Islander teachers in the nineteenth century, African catechists, Bishop Crowther’s Niger Mission, Korean missionaries to Shandong in 1913 — but organised majority-world sending as a self-conscious movement began in India. In 1903 Tamil Christians in Tirunelveli formed the Indian Missionary Society, sending V. S. Azariah to the Telugu-speaking Dornakal area in 1909; in 1905 the National Missionary Society was founded at Serampore with the motto ‘Indian men, Indian money, Indian leadership’. Azariah’s speech at Edinburgh 1910 — ‘Give us friends!’ — became a classic protest against missionary paternalism.

After decolonisation the call for self-reliance grew sharper. In 1971 the Kenyan Presbyterian John Gatu proposed a moratorium on Western missionaries and funds so that African churches could find their own identity, a debate taken up at the WCC’s Bangkok conference (1973) and the All Africa Conference of Churches (1974). Evangelicals answered differently, by mobilising non-Western missionaries: Lausanne 1974 gave majority-world leaders such as René Padilla, Samuel Escobar and Festo Kivengere a global platform, and associations multiplied — the Evangelical Missionary Society of ECWA in Nigeria (1948), Calvary Ministries (CAPRO, 1975) and the Nigeria Evangelical Missions Association (1982); the Indian Evangelical Mission (1965), Friends Missionary Prayer Band (1958) and India Missions Association (1977); the Philippine Missions Association (1983); and COMIBAM, whose 1987 congress in São Paulo declared that Latin America had moved ‘from mission field to mission force’.

Indian mission is the largest and most distinctive branch: tens of thousands of Indian workers, mostly from the Christian south and northeast, serve cross-culturally among other language groups in north India, a form of mission that is foreign in culture but domestic in geography. In Nigeria and Ghana, denominational churches such as the Redeemed Christian Church of God (founded 1952; led from 1981 by Enoch Adeboye), Deeper Life Bible Church, Winners’ Chapel and Ghana’s Church of Pentecost planted congregations across Africa and among the diaspora; the RCCG claims parishes in well over a hundred countries. Brazilian Baptists, Assemblies of God and the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God followed Portuguese-speaking links to Angola, Mozambique and Portugal, and Brazilian missionaries went to Japan among Japanese-Brazilian migrants and to the Muslim world.

Migration became a mission strategy in its own right. Filipino domestic workers, nurses and seamen — millions of overseas Filipino workers — formed churches in the Gulf, Hong Kong and Europe, and Filipino agencies trained them as ‘tentmakers’. African-led churches became the largest congregations in London (Kingsway International Christian Centre, founded 1992 by the Nigerian Matthew Ashimolowo), while the Nigerian pastor Sunday Adelaja founded the Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations in Kyiv in 1994, at its height one of Europe’s largest churches. Scholars such as Andrew Walls, Lamin Sanneh, Jehu Hanciles and Kwame Bediako argued that the centre of gravity of Christianity had shifted south, and that ‘reverse mission’ to secular Europe was a real if partial phenomenon — most migrant congregations remain largely ethnic.

The Center for the Study of Global Christianity estimated around 400,000 international missionaries in 2010, with the United States still the largest sender (about 127,000), followed by Brazil (about 34,000) and several European countries and South Korea (about 20,000 each), with India in the top ten. Lausanne’s third congress in Cape Town (2010) and fourth in Incheon (2024) were shaped by majority-world leadership. Critics have noted that the new missions sometimes reproduced Western faults — denominational competition, dependency on foreign funds, ethnocentrism and neglect of member care — and that some exported prosperity and ‘Word of Faith’ teaching or authoritarian ‘big man’ leadership, while defenders stress their cultural nearness, simplicity and willingness to work among the poor and in hostile contexts.
missions/majority-world-missions/beliefs: The Great Commission is binding on every church, not only on Western churches, and a ‘mission field’ church is not mature until it sends missionaries.
Mission should be from everywhere to everywhere, including to secularised Europe and North America.
Evangelical convictions about conversion, the Bible and the uniqueness of Christ, often combined with Pentecostal expectations of healing, power and spiritual warfare.
The dignity and capacity of non-Western Christians to lead, theologise and fund mission without foreign control.
Holistic mission (integral mission) linking evangelism with education, health and justice, particularly in Latin American and African voices.
In some neo-Pentecostal networks, prosperity and ‘dominion’ teaching that frames mission as conquest of territories and spheres of society.
missions/majority-world-missions/strateg: National missionary societies funded by local giving, such as the Indian Missionary Society (1903) and National Missionary Society (1905).
Denominational mission boards and church-planting networks that open branches wherever members migrate (RCCG, Church of Pentecost, Assemblies of God).
Prayer-band and support-group models in which ordinary church members pledge regular support for a missionary family (FMPB).
Tentmaking and diaspora mission through migrant workers, students and professionals.
National and continental mission associations (NEMA, IMA, PMA, COMIBAM, KWMA) for training, research and coordination.
Cross-cultural mission within large multilingual nations, especially India, Nigeria and Indonesia.
missions/majority-world-missions/groupsR: North Indian Hindi-belt communities, Adivasis and Dalits, reached by South Indian and Northeastern Indian missionaries.
Muslim-majority peoples of northern Nigeria, the Sahel and North Africa, reached by Nigerian and Ghanaian agencies.
Lusophone Africa and Portugal, through Brazilian churches and agencies.
Japanese-Brazilians in Japan and Brazilian migrants worldwide.
Gulf-state migrant communities and East Asian domestic workers, through Filipino churches.
Secularised populations of Western Europe and post-Soviet Eastern Europe through African-led churches.
missions/majority-world-missions/challen: Limited funds and currency weakness, making overseas work expensive and missionaries financially insecure.
Visa restrictions, anti-conversion laws and persecution in many receiving countries.
Inadequate training and pastoral care, leading to high attrition and burnout.
Dependence on Western agencies or funding in some cases, raising questions of autonomy.
Ethnic insularity of diaspora churches, which often struggle to reach the host population.
The tension between growth-focused strategies and integral, culturally sensitive mission.
missions/majority-world-missions/harms/0: Export of prosperity and Word of Faith teaching from some Nigerian, Ghanaian, Brazilian and Korean churches, encouraging exploitative giving and spiritual manipulation.
missions/majority-world-missions/harms/1: Reproduction of denominational rivalry, ethnocentrism and paternalism toward the peoples served — critiques once made of Western missions.
missions/majority-world-missions/harms/2: Authoritarian ‘big man’ leadership and financial scandals in some transnational churches, such as the Ukrainian investigations surrounding Sunday Adelaja’s associates in 2008.
missions/majority-world-missions/harms/3: Aggressive evangelism that has inflamed communal tensions in India, Nigeria and elsewhere and has been used by opponents to justify anti-conversion laws.
missions/majority-world-missions/harms/4: Witchcraft and deliverance teaching carried into diaspora settings, linked in a few notorious cases to the abuse of children accused of witchcraft.
missions/majority-world-missions/develop: Ended the identification of Christian mission with the West and with colonial power.
Brought missionaries culturally and economically closer to the peoples they serve, often at lower cost.
Produced majority-world missiology (Azariah, Padilla, Escobar, Bediako, Sanneh, Walls’ African colleagues) that reshaped global mission thinking.
Revitalised Christianity in European cities through migrant churches.
Created new forms of mission partnership and research, such as national mission associations and the Lausanne movement’s global networks.
Gave dignity and agency to non-Western Christians as givers, not merely receivers, in the world church.
missions/majority-world-missions/outcome: By the 2020s most of the world’s Christians and a large and growing share of its missionaries lived in Africa, Asia and Latin America, and global mission had become a polycentric, multidirectional movement.

missions/majority-world-missions/countri: India

The Indian Missionary Society (1903), National Missionary Society (1905), FMPB, IEM and the India Missions Association made India one of the largest sources of cross-cultural missionaries, mostly serving within India.
Nigeria
The Evangelical Missionary Society (1948), CAPRO (1975), NEMA (1982) and transnational churches such as the RCCG, Deeper Life and Winners’ Chapel sent workers across Africa and to the diaspora.
Ghana
The Church of Pentecost, rooted in James McKeown’s work from 1937 and Ghanaian-led since 1982, planted branches in over a hundred countries.
Brazil
The Brazilian Baptist Junta de Missões Mundiais (1907), COMIBAM (1987) and Pentecostal churches made Brazil one of the top missionary senders.
Philippines
The Philippine Missions Association (1983) mobilised overseas Filipino workers as tentmakers in the Gulf, Asia and Europe.
South Korea
Korea’s missionary force grew from under a hundred in 1979 to about 20,000 in the 2010s.
United Kingdom
African-led churches such as KICC (1992) and the RCCG became among the largest and fastest-growing congregations in London.
Ukraine
Sunday Adelaja’s Embassy of God in Kyiv became a symbol of African ‘reverse mission’ to Europe.
Kenya
John Gatu’s call for a moratorium on missionaries began a continental debate on self-reliance.
Mozambique and Angola
Brazilian Pentecostal and neo-Pentecostal churches expanded after independence, using the Portuguese language and media.
missions/majority-world-missions/journey: V. S. Azariah goes to Dornakal for the Indian Missionary Society

Tamil Christians funded and sent their own missionary to the Telugu-speaking Nizam’s territory; Azariah was consecrated in 1912 as Bishop of Dornakal, the first Indian bishop of the Anglican communion.
Sunday Adelaja from Nigeria to Kyiv

Adelaja went to the Soviet Union to study journalism in Minsk, became a Christian worker after the collapse of communism, and in 1994 founded the church in Kyiv that became an emblem of ‘reverse mission’.
The Lausanne congresses move south and east
The movement’s four global congresses traced the shift of evangelical mission leadership toward Asia and Africa.
missions/majority-world-missions/relatio: Majority-world agencies and leaders became the centre of Lausanne’s networks from Manila 1989 onwards.
Pacific churches such as the Tongan, Samoan and Fijian Methodists and Congregationalists continue a long tradition of Islander sending within the modern movement.
missions/majority-world-missions/agreeme: Shared the priority of evangelism, the unreached-peoples focus and the integration of social responsibility affirmed in the Lausanne Covenant.
Fulfilled Venn’s goal of churches that are not only self-supporting and self-governing but self-propagating, sending missionaries themselves.
Shared the post-colonial critique of paternalism and the call, voiced from Azariah to Gatu, for genuine partnership between older and younger churches.
missions/majority-world-missions/disagre: Most majority-world evangelical agencies rejected the 1970s moratorium proposal and the WCC’s emphasis on dialogue in favour of active evangelism and church-planting.
Majority-world missiologists criticised Western strategic metrics, ‘closure’ language and managerial missiology as culturally foreign and reductive.
Hosts in Africa, Asia and Latin America have questioned whether Western short-term trips create dependency and serve visitors more than local churches.
missions/majority-world-missions/deviati: Prosperity and Word of Faith teaching in some sending churches departs from the self-sacrificial vision of early indigenous mission societies like the IMS and NMS.
Some transnational churches serve chiefly their own diaspora and denominational expansion rather than cross-cultural evangelism, diverging from the ‘everywhere to everywhere’ ideal.
Dependence on Western money in some agencies contradicts the founding principle of self-support (‘Indian men, Indian money’).
Territorial spiritual-warfare and dominion theologies in some networks go beyond mainstream evangelical teaching.
